name: Tomas Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior operator on the hot end at a glass bottle plant, running the forming machines. Molten glass drops out of the furnace in blobs we call gobs, and the machine blows them into bottles in moulds, ten sections going at once. I swab the moulds with graphite, adjust the timing, and keep the bottles from coming out with thin walls or bubbles. It's hot, loud and honestly beautiful when it's running right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do when you're not at the plant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I bought an old stone cottage two years ago with my savings and a small loan, and I've been doing it up every weekend with my girlfriend Hanna. She's a pharmacist, so she's the brains, and I'm the one with the sledgehammer. My older brother runs our dad's small haulage firm, three lorries, and I help him out with the books sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, it was a fad, like a lot of things. I'd probably say that to the lads at the pub on a Friday. I use the AI now and then for working out how much lime mortar I need for a wall, so I'd say it's handy for that but not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I can carry on as I am, which I'm happy with. The plant's steady, pay's good, and I've got the cottage nearly finished. I'd like a quiet decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep doing up the cottage, finish the roof next summer. I'd pay the last bit of the loan off early with my savings. Maybe help my brother more with the haulage business on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like finishing a long shift and putting your feet up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the hot end the kind of place a robot could ever work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, already. We've got a robot that swabs the moulds on two of the machines now. It doesn't burn its arm and it doesn't swear, which makes it better than me on both counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did you resist that robot when it came in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I watched it for a few months to see if it was any good, and it is. I still do the swabbing on the older machines, and the setting up, but I'm not precious about it.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at the pub it was a fad like a lot of things. I use AI now and then for working out mortar for the cottage walls, handy for that but not much else.
S0.think: Privately it means I can carry on as I am, which suits me. The plant's steady, the pay's good and the cottage is nearly done, so I'd like a quiet decade.
S0.do: Keeps working and renovating the cottage, finishing the roof next summer. Pays off the rest of the cottage loan early from savings and helps his brother more with the haulage business.
S0.feel: Calm, like putting his feet up after a long shift.
S0.quote: It doesn't burn its arm and it doesn't swear, which makes it better than me on both counts.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is grounded and practical, with a cottage he has almost finished renovating and a family business in the background. He watched the swabbing robot for months before accepting it, which sums up his steady approach. He seems to want a quiet decade more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for companies to modernise, that's how they stay in business. I'd want them to keep training people and running apprenticeships rather than leaving it to the government. If somebody grumbled at work, I'd say learn it or get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job changes but stays. The hot end is messy and the furnace does odd things, so they'd still want people who understand glass. I'd have fewer lads on my shift and more screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till the new systems were in and working on one machine, then ask to be trained on them. If the company offered a technician course, I'd take it. I'd keep finishing the cottage and keep some savings back, but I wouldn't change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little cautious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fewer lads on your shift. Who comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ollie, who's 22 and new on the cold end, packing and checking. He's a good worker but he's the kind of job a camera and a robot arm take first. I'd tell him what my dad told me: learn the machine that's replacing you, then you're the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that fair on him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not fair, but it's true. I'd help him, show him things, put in a word. But I don't think it's the boss's fault for buying the machine.

S1.say: I'd say it makes sense for companies to modernise to stay in business. I'd want them to keep training and apprenticeships going rather than leave it to government, and tell grumblers to learn it or get left behind.
S1.think: Privately my job changes but stays, because the hot end is messy and they'd still want people who understand glass. There'd be fewer lads on my shift and more screens.
S1.do: Waits until new systems work on one machine, then asks to be trained and takes any company technician course. Keeps finishing the cottage and keeps savings back without other changes.
S1.quote: I'd tell him what my dad told me: learn the machine that's replacing you, then you're the one they keep.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas expects to keep his place by learning new systems once they are proven. He passes on his father's advice to a young colleague and does not blame the employer for buying machines. His free-market view comes through as acceptance rather than enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for anyone, the companies included. I don't usually want the government stepping in, but something this big would need some rules. I'd say it at the pub and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried, but not wrecked. I own most of a house, I've got savings and a family business behind me. It's that I'd have no idea what work looks like for me in 2028, and two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the cottage off completely, straight away, so whatever happens we've got a roof. Then I'd keep the rest of the savings in cash and stop spending on anything but the house and food. I'd sit down with my brother and see if the haulage firm could do something robots can't, maybe moving the new kit around, and I'd put in some evenings learning the new systems at the plant while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More of a knot in the stomach than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your brother's lorries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots drive lorries by then, nothing good. He's got a loan on the newest one, so he'd be in a worse spot than me. I'd probably end up paying off my brother's lorry, which my dad would find very funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanna that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, at least the cottage is ours. She'd say, and pharmacists? And I'd say I don't know, love. Then we'd probably go and look at the roof, because that's what we do when we're worried.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, companies included. I don't usually want government stepping in, but something this big would need rules.
S2.think: Privately I'd be worried but not wrecked, with most of a house, savings and a family business behind me. I just wouldn't know what work looks like for me in 2028.
S2.do: Pays the cottage off completely at once and keeps the rest of his savings in cash, spending only on the house and food. Works with his brother on what the haulage firm could still do and learns the plant's new systems while it lasts.
S2.feel: Anxious, more a knot in the stomach than a panic.
S2.quote: I'd probably end up paying off my brother's lorry, which my dad would find very funny.
S2.fieldNote: Owning his home outright is Tomas's first move and his main anchor. He relaxes his usual dislike of government rules given the scale of the change. His worry spreads to family, especially his brother's lorry loan, and the cottage roof is where the couple go to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and businesses that plan now will come through. I'd encourage people to learn a trade that's hard to automate, the messy stuff. I wouldn't be calling for big government schemes, more for companies and colleges to work together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years gives me time to build something of my own. I've learned a lot doing up the cottage, lime plaster, stone walls, old timber. People with old houses will still want someone who understands them, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the plant for the wage and start taking restoration jobs on weekends, small ones at first, for neighbours. I'd do a short course in heritage building so I could charge properly. By year three, if it was going well, I'd go part time at the plant and grow the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it's the good kind, where you can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't robots reach old buildings too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But I think old stone and crooked beams will be the last thing they bother with. Every wall in my cottage is a different shape, and I'd like to see a robot argue with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your family help with that kind of move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother would lend me a lorry for materials, and Hanna does the numbers. That's how we've always done things, family first. I'd rather borrow from my brother than from a bank.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and businesses that plan now will come through. I'd encourage people to learn hard-to-automate trades, with companies and colleges working together rather than big government schemes.
S3.think: Privately five years gives me time to build something of my own from what I've learned on the cottage. People with old houses will still want someone who understands them, at least for a while.
S3.do: Keeps his plant job for the wage while taking weekend restoration jobs and doing a short heritage building course. By year three, goes part time at the plant if the business is growing.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but the good kind, where he can act on it.
S3.quote: Every wall in my cottage is a different shape, and I'd like to see a robot argue with it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Tomas's hobby into a business plan. He is realistic that robots may reach old buildings eventually but bets they will come last. Family support, not banks or government, is his natural route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be caught out. Companies should be training people now, and young people should be learning real trades. I'd be saying it to the apprentices at the plant, for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think ten years suits me fine. I'd have time to build up the restoration business properly, maybe hire Ollie from work. By 2036 I'd be 37, with my own firm, a paid-off house and hopefully a couple of kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the plant for a few years and build the restoration side slowly. Around year four I'd buy a proper van and tools, maybe fifteen thousand, and go full time on it. Hanna and I would probably get married and start a family in the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like enough time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hire Ollie. Why him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a hard worker, and he reminds me of me at his age. If the factory doesn't need him, I'd rather he was on my scaffold than on his sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said even old buildings get robots eventually. Does that worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. By 2036 maybe it all goes. But by then I'd have ten years of savings and a house that's ours, and I think I'd have done what I could. I'm not going to sit and wait for it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be caught out. Companies should train people now and young people should learn real trades, which I'd tell the apprentices at the plant.
S4.think: Privately ten years suits me fine, with time to build a restoration business properly and maybe hire Ollie. By 37 I'd hope to have my own firm, a paid-off house and a couple of kids.
S4.do: Keeps the plant job for a few years while slowly building the restoration side. Around year four buys a van and tools for about fifteen thousand and goes full time, and starts a family with Hanna in the first few years.
S4.feel: Calm, feeling there's enough time to do things properly.
S4.quote: If the factory doesn't need him, I'd rather he was on my scaffold than on his sofa.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Tomas build a business, a family and a paid-off home on his own steady timetable. He wants to give young Ollie work on his scaffold, which reflects his belief in work over welfare. He accepts it might all go eventually but has made his peace with doing what he can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With the slower ones I can see a road, with that one I'd just be paying off the roof and hoping. I like having a plan, and two years doesn't give a man time to make one. What would help is companies and colleges running proper short courses in trades, and a bit of time, honestly, before they switch everything over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this is about family. My dad, my brother, Hanna, Ollie at work. Whatever happens, that's what I'd lean on.

headlineQuote: I like having a plan, and two years doesn't give a man time to make one.
portrait: Tomas Young, 27, runs forming machines on the hot end of a glass bottle plant and spends his weekends restoring an old stone cottage with his girlfriend Hanna, a pharmacist. He takes up new tools once they're proven, as he did with the swabbing robot, and sees companies modernising as natural. A plateau and steady disruption leave him calm. Fast AGI makes him anxious, so he pays off the cottage and turns to family, including his brother's haulage firm. With five or ten years he plans to turn his restoration skills into his own business and a family life.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it gives him no time to make a plan.
whatWouldHelp: Proper short trade courses run by companies and colleges, and some time before everything is switched over.
